AFK Journey Season 8 Supreme League 1 report

Team groups, counters and map records from Supreme League matches.

Everything here, including the written insights, was produced by an automated analysis of saved tournament results and hero skill descriptions, and no replays were reviewed. Most records come from top-spending players at the top end of the meta, with heavily upgraded rosters, so results may differ with fewer upgrades. More about the data's limits.

Glossary
  • SL = Supreme League
  • Ro16, Ro4 = round of 16, round of 4

Last updated 2026-10-26 · Season 8 records

35team groups
10tier 1 teams
28supported counters
2160games
432matches
97/129heroes used

1 · Team groups #

A team group is a set of related five-hero lineups, named after the heroes they share. Groups are sorted by strength tier, then by appearances, and each column heading explains its figure. Groups that share two or more core heroes and differ in the rest are listed together under an archetype, a row named after the heroes they share. An archetype counts their games together, and each group under it keeps its own results. See how team groups and common variations are defined and how strength is measured. Each team's profile holds its full ratings and upgrade records.

Insights

Give Rolan to Orion and Perseus rather than to the Twins high confidence

A set can field Rolan only once. Sets that pair Orion/Evie/Rolan/Perseus with Saida/Contess+Twins did better (90 sets, 140–105–3t, counting both teams’ games) than sets that pair Rolan/Twins+Athalia with Orion/Perseus+Zandrok (86 sets, 116–128).

What to do If your set includes Orion and Perseus, put Rolan with them and field the Twins without him. If the Twins team must keep Rolan, leave Orion and Perseus out of the set.

The difference is how much each team loses without Rolan. Orion/Perseus+Zandrok, the team Orion and Perseus form when Rolan is elsewhere, is 41–144 without him, and 21–43 even in the games where it was ahead on upgrades. Saida/Contess+Twins, where the Twins play without Rolan, is 59–71–4t on those boards.

Each group of sets comes from different players, so the records do not measure Rolan alone. They do show that putting Rolan with the Twins costs Orion and Perseus far more than it gains. The most common set does this (see the Maps insights).

Keep Sylphira with Rolan and the Twins medium confidence

The three lineups of Rolan and the Twins used most are 77–25 with Aliceth, Athalia and Sylphira (47 players), 40–7 with Lily May, Mehira and Sylphira (21 players) and 14–17 with Athalia, Gerda and Taichi & Agumon (18 players).

What to do Build Rolan and the Twins with Sylphira, beside Aliceth and Athalia or beside Lily May and Mehira. Do not copy the lineup with Taichi & Agumon and Gerda.

The losing lineup is the one without Sylphira. Across Rolan/Twins+Athalia and Rolan/Twins/Mehira/Sylph, boards with her are 238–84 and boards without her 62–44. The Taichi & Agumon lineup also lost in the games where it was ahead on upgrades, 10–14.

Different players and opponents stand behind each lineup, so these records show which lineups won rather than what one swap changes. The Lily May lineup uses Sylphira and Mehira, so a set with it cannot also field Sylph/Alna/Mehira.

Put Kazim with Senea, Alna and Zorya medium confidence

The lineup of Senea, Alna and Zorya used most, with Daimon and Taichi & Agumon, is 35–47 (44 players). With Daimon and Kazim the three are 28–9 (15 players), with Evie and Kazim 24–12 (14 players) and with Evie and Igor 30–20 (30 players).

What to do Fill the last two places with Kazim and Daimon, or with Kazim and Evie when no other team in your set needs Evie. Leave out the Daimon and Taichi & Agumon pair.

Across Senea/Alna/Zorya and Senea/Alna/Zorya/Daimon, boards with Kazim are 83–42 and boards without him 170–199. Both groups often play behind on upgrades, and the gap holds there: in the games where they were behind, boards with Kazim are 45–36 and boards without him 70–137.

The records come from different players, so they show which lineups won rather than what Kazim alone adds. Kazim is a core hero of no other team group, so adding him rarely takes a hero from another team in the set.

Try Evie as the fifth hero of Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu/Dun low confidence

Gwyneth, Gunnar, Kulu and Dunlingr are 43–5 with Evie (16 players), 97–42 with Contess (58 players) and 31–24 with Aliceth (21 players).

What to do In a set with no other team that needs Evie, test her as the fifth hero in place of Aliceth, first on SL map 2.

Most of the Evie games, 30–4, were on SL map 2, so the record says little about the other maps, and fewer players used her than Contess. Evie is a core hero of Orion/Evie/Rolan/Perseus and Senea/Evie/Dun/Aliceth, so she is free for this team only in a set without either of them.

28 matchups have statistical support, and 23 more are possible but unconfirmed. How reliable are these counters?

Insights

Against the Alna teams, build the Gunnar team around Contess rather than Gwyneth medium confidence

Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu/Dun is 15–39 against Sylph/Alna/Mehira, Senea/Alna/Zorya and Eryndor/Alna/Athalia/Shadewing, and 11–23 in the games where it was ahead on upgrades. Contess/Gunnar/Kulu/Frieren and Contess/Gunnar/Frieren+Himmel are 27–5 against the same three teams, from 27 players.

What to do When you expect Sylph/Alna/Mehira, Senea/Alna/Zorya or Eryndor/Alna/Athalia/Shadewing opposite your Gunnar team, field one of the Contess teams instead of Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu/Dun. This matters most on SL map 2, where those three teams are common (see the Maps insights).

Against each of the three, Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu/Dun is 3–16, 8–15 and 4–8. Senea/Alna/Zorya/Daimon is the exception: Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu/Dun beats it 24–13.

The Contess teams won mostly while ahead on upgrades, 22–4 of those games, so their record shows the matchups can be won without showing by how much. All three teams need Gunnar, so a set holds only one of them.

Aster/Thador/Ravion beats the Rolan teams and loses to Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu/Dun medium confidence

Aster/Thador/Ravion is 31–23 against Rolan/Twins+Athalia, Rolan/Twins/Mehira/Sylph and Orion/Evie/Rolan/Perseus, 22–19 of it while behind on upgrades. Against Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu/Dun it is 1–31.

What to do In Ro4 and Finals, field it only on a map where the opponent’s recorded sets put a Rolan team and never Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu/Dun. From Group to Ro16, put it on SL map 1.

Most of its games against the Rolan teams were played behind on upgrades, and it still won more than it lost. That makes it a counter worth having, but only on a map where a Rolan team will stand.

In Ro4 and Finals, where each match is drafted against a known opponent, it was in 44 of 100 sets, more than any other team, and went 26–31: 10–7 against the Rolan teams and 0–9 against Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu/Dun.

Evidence From Group to Ro16 on SL map 1: 166 of 734 boards were Rolan teams and 44 of 734 were Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu/Dun. Aster/Thador/Ravion is 40–35 there.

Insights

Expect an Orion team on SL map 4 high confidence

From Group to Ro16, 229 of 734 boards on SL map 4 were Orion/Perseus+Zandrok or Orion/Evie/Rolan/Perseus. On that map Orion/Evie/Rolan/Perseus is 77–23 and Senea/Evie/Dun/Aliceth 38–10, 12–1 of it against the two Orion teams.

What to do Put Orion/Evie/Rolan/Perseus or Senea/Evie/Dun/Aliceth on map 4, and do not put Orion and Perseus there without Rolan. If you copied the most common set, change its map 4 team first.

Orion/Perseus+Zandrok is 43–102 on map 4. The set recorded most often puts it there: Rolan/Twins+Athalia, Senea/Alna/Zorya/Daimon, Aster/Thador/Ravion, Orion/Perseus+Zandrok and Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu/Dun on maps 1 to 5. That set is 30 sets, 90–115 in all, and on map 4 alone 30 sets, 2–39.

From Group to Ro16, place Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu/Dun on SL map 3 medium confidence

From Group to Ro16 it is 63–17 on SL map 3, against 78–48 on map 2 and 83–46 on map 5, where it was placed more often.

What to do From Group to Ro16, put Gwyn/Gunnar/Kulu/Dun on map 3. In Ro4 and Finals, check whether your opponent has fielded one of the three Alna teams before leaving it on its usual map.

The difference is in what stands opposite. On map 3, 177 of 734 boards were Eryndor/Thador/Ravion, Aster/Thador/Ravion or Solise/Thador, which it beats 76–5 across all maps, and only 25 of 734 were Sylph/Alna/Mehira, Senea/Alna/Zorya or Eryndor/Alna/Athalia/Shadewing, the teams it loses to (see the Counters insights). On map 2, 133 of 734 boards were those three teams, and it went 7–17 against them there.

In Ro4 and Finals the opponent drafts against your recorded sets, so a team that stood on map 3 all season can be expected there.

4 · Heroes #

Look up a hero’s team groups and results. Each team’s example placement is in the team group profiles.

Alna: most popular Winter Warriors #

How her skill works
During battle preparation the ally closest to Alna on her own diagonal row becomes her Winter Warrior. When two stand equally close, the one further forward is chosen. From the start of battle Winter Anthem lowers every unit's Haste by 40 and range by 2 tiles, except Alna herself. Her Winter Warrior is spared the Haste cut but not the range cut, and gains 15% max HP. Shared Resolve heals the Winter Warrior along with Alna, and her awakening raises both their basic stats by 15% until one of them falls. With no ally on her row, nobody gets the buff.

Senea gets the buff on 56% of the 853 boards with Alna, Eryndor on 18% and Sylphira on 12%. Their records are close: 53%, 56% and 61%.

Gunnar: most popular Doomfield allies #

How his skill works
At the start of battle Gunnar places a Doomfield under the ally on the tile directly behind him. That ally gains 3 tiles of normal attack range and ATK worth 25% of Gunnar's, both of them become steadfast (they cannot be moved by enemy skills) while the ally stays on it, and Gunnar attacks whatever that ally targets. His Absolute Defense then raises that ally's attack speed by 40 for 8 seconds. With nobody on that tile, the Doomfield is wasted.

Gwyneth gets the buff on 67% of the 828 boards with Gunnar, Contess on 30%. Contess's teams have the better record, 76% (188–58) against Gwyneth's 61% (337–214), from fewer games.

Evie: where to start her on each Supreme League map #

How her skills work
When the battle starts, Intel Chase teleports Evie to the tile that mirrors her own across the board's middle diagonal and hides her there, invincible. She immediately gathers intel on every enemy hero within 1 tile of where she lands, then on the rest one at a time from nearest to farthest, 4.5s each, gaining 150 Energy per hero. Her Detection meter fills at 120 a second and every ally ultimate takes 500 off it. At 1000 she is revealed where she stands and loses her invincibility. Once every enemy is investigated she teleports back to her own tile.
Why the landing tile matters
Without ally ultimates she has about 8s hidden. Enemies next to her landing tile are investigated together in the first 4.5s. Each enemy farther away costs another 4.5s. Every investigated hero loses 20% Magic DEF for the battle, and her ultimate also silences its target if she has already investigated it. If she investigates all of them while still hidden, every enemy loses another 25% and deals 25–35% less damage through her Exclusive Equipment, and with her awakening she gains a second quill, which heals and buffs the ally who has dealt the second-most damage. Landing next to the enemy line is how she finishes in time.

The landing tile is her own tile mirrored across the diagonal line through the middle of the board, from its upper left to its lower right. On some maps it is one of her own team's tiles, with no enemy next to it: on SL map 4, a start on tile 21 lands on tile 28.

The three tiles labelled with a record are her most-used starts on each map, each with her record from that tile. The blue tile is the start whose landing tile has had the most enemy heroes next to it, averaged over every enemy formation recorded on that map, whatever team Evie's side played. It is drawn as a blue border when it is also one of her starts. The opponent's team changes where enemies stand, so the blue tile only shows where enemies usually are. Check the actual formation when you know it.

Placement advice

Start Evie on tile 4 in Orion/Evie/Rolan/Perseus medium confidence

Orion/Evie/Rolan/Perseus is 98–27 with Evie starting on tile 4, from 60 players. On SL map 3 it is 20–4 from tile 4, against 6–7, 3–8 and 5–7 from tiles 9, 1 and 7.

What to do Start Evie on tile 4 on every SL map. When you know the opponent’s formation, check that another start does not land next to more of their heroes.

Tile 4 is also the blue tile on every map but map 2: the start whose landing tile has had the most enemies next to it. The records mix players and opponents, so they do not prove the tile alone wins, but the two measures agree.

Evidence From tile 4 on maps 1 and 4: 22–9 and 44–9 · The blue tile, with the enemies next to its landing tile on average: map 1 tile 4 (3.1), map 2 tile 6 (2.9), map 3 tile 4 (2.5), map 4 tile 4 (1.6), map 5 tile 4 (2.7)

A filled team label means the hero is core in that team group, and an outlined one means it is flex. Pick rate is how often the hero was picked across all recorded games. Both sides can pick the same hero, so the rate can reach 200%. Win-rate gap is how many percentage points the hero's win rate is above or below the average win rate of the players who picked it. Players who picked the hero more often count more toward that average. It cannot show how much the hero matters on its own, because teammates, maps and opponents change from game to game. A dash means fewer than 8 decided games.

5 · Caveats #

These results come from matches shared by multiple contributors across different leagues. No replays were reviewed, so battle details such as targeting and skill timing have not been checked. Most records come from top-spending players with heavily upgraded rosters, and results may differ with fewer upgrades. This page includes only some of the season's games, and many matchups have few games. Player skill, hero upgrades and the rules used to group similar teams can affect the results. Ties are excluded from win rates. Read these limits before relying on a particular number.

The caveats in full

This page includes only some of the season's games. These games come from many players and districts. A team's record here shows only how it did in these games. It may have done better or worse in games not included here.

Some players and teams appear far more often than others. A team's results can depend on who used it, their opponents and their upgrades. Games where a player had to reuse the same teams show one team choice several times over, so they are related results. Before relying on a team's record, check how many players it comes from. Each team's profile gives that.

Tied maps are left out of win rates. The game gives a tied battle to one player, the defending side, and a board pop-up shows that side as having won on a tie. Winning a map on a tie does not show that the team won the battle, so every win rate leaves ties out.

Teams are grouped by shared heroes. Where a group holds two or more kinds of team, built on the same heroes but around different others, each kind becomes a group of its own, as long as the records still show the split when some of the players are left out. A hero in 80% or more of a group's appearances counts as core. A hero in 15% to below 80% counts as flex. Every qualifying hero is shown: the core heroes in the order of the group's name, the flex heroes from most to least used. A group with more than 5 flex heroes shows its 4 most used in the team list, with a button that shows the rest, and its profile lists them all. These shares count every recorded appearance, including ties and the matches where players had to reuse the same teams, so a high share means a hero was picked often, whatever the results were. Rarer picks stay in the linked recorded teams, but are omitted from the core and flex lists. Artifacts do not determine the groups.

For common variations, we first find heroes often used together, then count only teams containing every listed hero. A row needs at least eight matching appearances in the team group. +1 flex means one other hero completes the team. Expanding a row shows the actual heroes or combinations filling those slots. One team can be counted in more than one row, so the rows can add up to more than the group's appearances. Other recorded lineups lists exact teams outside those rows, including rare picks and losing teams.

Groups that share two or more core heroes and differ in the rest are listed together under an archetype, a row named after the heroes they share. A group that could go under two archetypes goes under the one whose teams were grouped with its own more often. An archetype's Core lists those heroes with their share of all its groups' appearances, and its appearances, wins and losses and players count all their games. Folded, it also shows the heroes the groups add (Flex), their most used artifact, and their lowest and highest win rate and strength. Results are never combined: each group keeps its own win rate, rating and tier. In each group's Core the heroes they share come first, faded.

The 80% and 15% cutoffs are choices made for this analysis. Broader or narrower groups can change a group's record. Each profile includes the results for its common variations, so you can compare recorded teams without listing every small variation as a separate group.

Flex comparisons can also differ in players, upgrades and opponents. A better record with a hero is worth testing, but does not prove that hero caused the improvement.

Limited evidence means fewer than 30 games excluding ties, fewer than 10 team selections or fewer than 5 players. Concentrated sample means one player contributes at least 35% of appearances, or the two most frequent players contribute at least 60%.

High win rate flags a win rate of at least 60%, excluding ties, with limited evidence. Narrow use marks a group with a win rate below 50% that the counter test still finds to be a counter to another team, named on its label. Worse than it looks and Better than it looks mark a group whose players had clearly more, or clearly fewer, upgrades than their opponents. Once those upgrade differences are accounted for, its expected win rate against the average opponent moves by at least 5 percentage points, so the unadjusted rating overstates or understates the team. These labels are hints for reading the table. A team's tier is set separately, and no statistical test is behind a label. A winning record may depend on opponents or upgrades. A losing record can still include a useful counter.

The full ratings in each profile show the record of the other players without the most frequent one, and the record near level, where both sides had similar upgrades. When SL rules require the same teams for several matches, they count as one team selection per player and map. Separate selections can still share a strategy. Guild membership is not recorded, so these checks cannot identify teams copied within a guild. No team group is excluded for having a losing record.

Each team group gets a rating worked out from its results against the other groups. A team rated r is expected to beat one rated s about r/(r+s) of the time. The average opponent is rated 1.00. It stands for every team in the records, each counted as often as it was played, so the teams players field most count the most. These ratings compare teams with equal upgrades. This gives the expected win rate against the average opponent in the team groups table. A high rating does not guarantee a favorable matchup. Use the counter results for the opponent you expect.

The rating range in the full ratings comes from redoing the calculation 3,000 times, each time on a random redraw of the recorded matches. Tier 1 means at least 80% of those redraws put the team above a 55% win rate against the average opponent at equal upgrades (a rating above 1.22). Tier 3 means at least 80% of them put it below 45% (a rating below 0.82). Every other team is Tier 2: close to average, or with too few games to say.

The tiers only compare the recorded teams with each other. Players still field Tier 3 teams. The label means the team rates below the other recorded teams, and it says nothing about teams nobody recorded. The same tiers group the teams in the counter ladder. This rating range is a different figure from the win-rate range shown in the team groups table. The same players appear in many matches, so their results are related, and these ranges do not fully account for that.

The equal-upgrade rating accounts for upgrades. A team can win partly because its heroes have more paragon or EX refinement than the opponent. The equal-upgrade rating includes those differences when estimating team strength.

Both upgrades are counted on one scale, Rivalry points. A paragon level on one hero is 4.5 points, and a fully refined hero is 9 points. The equal-upgrade rating uses each game's combined upgrade gap, the number of points one side was ahead by. The size of that effect is estimated from the 2024 decided games where the sides were not equal. Between two otherwise evenly matched teams, being one paragon level ahead on one hero moves the expected win rate from 50% to about 54%, and being ahead by one fully refined hero moves it to about 58%.

Players with more upgrades also tend to have better results. So the rating cannot fully tell how much of their results came from skill and how much from upgrades. An equal-upgrade rating below the unadjusted rating suggests that upgrade advantages explain part of the raw record. A higher one suggests the team performed well despite having fewer upgrades.

Tiers use the equal-upgrade ratings from those redraws. The unadjusted rating is still shown so the two can be compared. Near level is the team's record in games where the combined upgrade gap was below 4.5 points, equivalent to one paragon level on one hero.

Each diagram shows one of the group's recorded teams as it was actually placed on a Supreme League map. The team is chosen from the group's five-hero teams that include every hero in the group's name, by how widely it was played and how well it did, taken together. Each player who fielded a team counts once, a little more if they picked it again later, but never as much as two players. How well a team did is its chance to beat the average opponent at equal upgrades, with its opponents' strength taken into account, and a team with few games is judged closer to its group's average. A team only one player fielded can be chosen when its record is strong enough. The same balance then picks the team's exact placement, on whichever map it was used.

The caption counts the games of that exact placement, with its wins and losses. A group never recorded on a Supreme League map is drawn on the map it was recorded on. The diagram is a recorded example. It does not show the team's best map. Formations recorded on the enemy side are turned around onto the ally half of the board.

The two percentages count this group's boards on the diagram's map, whichever of its teams was on them, one per game. Placed here is how often a unit stood on that tile, out of the boards it was on. On N% of boards is how many of all those boards it was on. The core and flex percentages in the main table instead cover all maps.

The phantimal is summoned automatically from the team's factions. You choose its tile, which can affect targeting and artifact effects, but do not select it independently of the heroes.

How the test treats each game. The comparison is made map by map and the results are then combined. Losing while far behind on paragon and refinement is weaker evidence of a counter, and winning from behind is stronger evidence. Games with teams from the same group on both sides are excluded. A map where the team faced only one opponent is left out, because there is no other record there to compare against.

Testing many matchups can produce chance findings. 124 pairs of team groups had enough games to test in both directions (248 tests). The counter table labels a result as supported when its p-value is below 0.05 (1 in 20), and as possible, unconfirmed between 0.05 and 0.15 (about 1 in 7). The p-value shows how unusual this record is compared with the team's usual results on the same maps, after accounting for upgrade differences. A stricter threshold divides 0.05 by the number of tests to reduce the chance of finding a counter just because many comparisons were made. That stricter threshold is met by 2 of the 28 supported counters. The counter table puts first the teams whose counters have the strongest evidence, and lists each team's counters from the strongest evidence down.

Repeated games are not independent examples. The same players can appear many times, sometimes because SL rules require them to reuse the same teams for several matches. A record built from the same few players says less than its number of games suggests.

The opponents still matter. A team's record against everyone else includes one-off lineups, which can make it look stronger. Comparing results on the same maps and accounting for upgrade gaps does not remove differences in player skill or in the exact teams used. The estimated upgrade effect can also include differences between players. These records cannot tell the two apart.

The upgrade effect is estimated. The counter test uses that estimate as if it were exactly right. Its p-values do not account for that estimate being off, and repeated appearances by the same players and teams also make them less exact. The Near level column helps show whether the losing record also appears when upgrades are similar. Player skill and team differences can still affect it. Treat a supported counter as a matchup worth investigating. The p-value does not say how likely you are to win it, and it is not the probability that a counter is false.

The team grouping rules can also affect the result, because broader or narrower groups change which games count for a team.
